events.text: A bank of black sand where the river bends north, warm in the day and cold at night. Under a hand's depth of sand, one egg, the colour of wet slate. Inside it, two hearts. One beats slowly, the way stones would beat if stones had hearts. The other beats quick and light, two beats to the slow one's one, and keeps trying to hurry it.
events.arc: The Egg in the Black Sand

choices.text: Listen to the slow heart and grow at its pace

effects.log: One beat, and a long pause, and one beat. The quick heart complains in little flutters. The slow heart does not hurry. You grow a shell before you grow anything else.

choices.text: Listen to the quick heart and grow at its pace

effects.log: Two beats for every one. The quick heart grows a tongue before it grows anything else, and tastes the sand through the shell, and learns that the river is to the north.

choices.text: Let the two hearts find a beat between them

effects.log: It takes most of the summer. In the end the slow heart beats a little faster and the quick one a little slower, and for a few nights at a time they beat together. Something in the egg is warm that was not warm before.

events.text: Something is digging in the sand above you: claws, and the grating of a beak, and a hungry little sound. A magpie has seen the sand disturbed where a turtle laid her eggs in the summer, and it has come to see what is under it. The other eggs of the clutch are already gone. Yours is the deepest.
events.arc: The Egg in the Black Sand

choices.text: Hold still. Be a stone in the sand

ok.log: The beak strikes something hard and round and dull, and the magpie decides it is a pebble. It goes away scolding. The slow heart did not speed up once.

fail.log: The beak finds the shell and knocks on it twice, and cracks it a hair. Then a boat comes round the bend and the magpie flies. The crack seals over in a week. (-10 health)

choices.text: Let the quick heart knock back from inside

effects.log: The quick heart beats against the inside of the shell like a fist on a door. The magpie hops back, tilts its head, and decides that an egg which knocks is not worth the trouble. Magpies are clever, but not that clever.

events.text: The first frost comes down over the black sand in the night, white on black, and the cold goes down through the sand to the egg. The quick heart slows. It slows too much. It is a snake's heart, and a snake's heart stops when it is cold enough, and does not always start again.
events.arc: The Egg in the Black Sand

choices.text: Wrap the slow warmth round the quick heart

effects.log: The slow heart has nothing to give but slowness, and it gives all of it. All night the quick heart beats once to every three of the slow one, very faint, held. In the morning the sun is on the sand and both hearts are beating.

choices.text: Let the quick heart fight the cold its own way

ok.log: The quick heart beats faster instead of slower, out of pure spite, until the egg is warm from inside. The slow heart is impressed, a little, and will never say so.

fail.log: The quick heart stops for a long, long moment, and the slow heart goes on alone in the dark. Then the quick one starts again, and neither of you will ever forget the silence. (-12 health)

events.text: Out. Black sand in your eyes, cold air, the river making its great noise a body's length away. You are the size of a coin and you have two heads, and the second one is a thread of black snake wound twice round your shell, and it is looking at you. You cannot tell where you stop and it starts. Neither can it. Somewhere down the bank a heron is walking.
events.arc: The Egg in the Black Sand

choices.text: The tortoise crawls toward the noise of the water, slowly

effects.log: One leg, the next leg, a rest. The snake hisses at every rest. You reach the water a long time after the snake would have, but you reach it, and the heron is looking the other way.

choices.text: The snake tastes the air and picks the way

effects.log: The snake tastes heron, and river, and something dead upstream, and steers you round all three by pulling on your shell like a rope. You reach the water fast and sideways and dizzy.

choices.text: Go together, the tortoise walking and the snake watching

effects.log: The tortoise walks; the snake watches the heron over your shell and says when to stop. It is the first thing you ever do together. The cold water closes over both your heads at once.

events.text: The first argument. The tortoise says the deep water is that way, because the bottom slopes that way. The snake says it is the other way, because it can taste cold coming from there. You are one body. You cannot go both ways. You sit on a pebble in the shallows for a whole afternoon going neither.

choices.text: Go the tortoise's way: the bottom does not lie

effects.log: The bottom slopes down into a pool, as the tortoise said. The snake says nothing all evening. It is a loud nothing.

choices.text: Go the snake's way: the cold does not lie either

effects.log: The cold comes from a spring under the bank, a good one, as the snake said. The tortoise says nothing all evening, which for the tortoise is not unusual, but this time it means something.

choices.text: Go neither way until you both agree

effects.log: At dusk you notice the pool and the spring are the same place, seen from two sides. Both heads were right. It is very annoying for both of them.

events.text: The first meal. A water snail on a stone: the tortoise has been working toward it since morning. A frog's tadpole flicks past and the snake takes it in one snap. Then a strange thing happens. The tortoise is full. You have one belly, and the snake has filled it, and the snail is still on the stone.

choices.text: Eat the snail anyway, out of principle

effects.log: You eat the snail very slowly, full, out of principle. The snake watches with interest. It has never seen anyone eat out of principle.

choices.text: Leave the snail. The snake hunts; the tortoise rests

effects.log: An arrangement, without anyone saying so. The snake catches; the tortoise digests. The snail on the stone lives to be very old.

choices.text: Both heads sit and think about what one belly means

effects.log: If the snake starves, so does the tortoise. If the tortoise is caught, so is the snake. You sit on the stone until dark with this thought between you like a third thing.

events.text: The snake's first lie. You are basking on a log, and the tortoise wants to go down, and the snake says: "The heron has gone. I watched it go." The heron has not gone. It is standing in the reeds ten lengths away, and the snake wants to stay in the sun.

choices.text: The tortoise looks for itself, and goes down anyway

effects.log: You slide off the log. The heron's beak goes into the water where you were a breath later. The snake says it must have come back. The tortoise says nothing at all.

choices.text: Believe the snake, and stay in the sun

ok.log: The heron does not see you, or does not care. You bask all afternoon. The snake learns that a lie can work. That is a bad thing to learn so young.

fail.log: The heron comes out of the reeds like a thrown spear. You drop off the log with a scrape across the shell. The tortoise will remember this one for a hundred years. (-10 health)

choices.text: Say it aloud, both heads: we do not lie to each other

effects.log: The snake looks at the tortoise for a long moment, and then down at the reeds, and says, "The heron is there." That is all. It is enough. You go down together.

events.text: Naming each other. Everything on the river has a name: the heron, the ford, the black-sand bank, the fat carp under the willow. The two of you have only ever said "you" to each other, and it has started to be a problem when you argue.

choices.text: The snake names the tortoise: Slow

effects.log: "Slow," says the snake. The tortoise thinks about it for three days and says: "Quick." Neither name is kind. Both stick.

choices.text: The tortoise names the snake: Thread

effects.log: The tortoise says "Thread," because the snake is the thread that holds the shell. The snake pretends to hate it, and answers to it at once.

choices.text: Name each other at the same moment

effects.log: You both speak at once, and neither of you hears the other's name for you, and you have to say them again. Stone, says the snake. Thread, says the tortoise. You lie on the riverbed afterwards feeling oddly shy.

events.text: A bad evening. A boy with a net on the bank, a heron on the other bank, the current pulling you toward the weir. And then, without a word, the tortoise turns left and the snake pulls left at the same moment, and you go between the net and the heron and over the low end of the weir like one thing, and it is like warmth, the first warmth of the year, inside the shell.

choices.text: Lie on the riverbed and feel it

effects.log: You lie in the cold under the weir and feel it until it fades. You will spend a great deal of your life trying to feel that again.

choices.text: The snake says it was luck

effects.log: "Luck," says the snake. The tortoise does not argue. Both of you know it was not.

choices.text: The tortoise says it was nothing

effects.log: "Nothing," says the tortoise, and draws its head in. The snake curls a little tighter round the shell, and does not argue. Both of you know it was not.

events.text: You have learned to sleep in turns. The tortoise sleeps in the long middle of the night, deep and still; the snake keeps watch, and counts the stars through the water, and wakes the tortoise if anything moves. Then the snake sleeps at dawn, in quick little naps, and the tortoise watches the light come. Tonight, for the first time, the snake does not wake you when the otter passes. It lets you sleep, and watches the otter alone.

choices.text: Pretend you did not wake

effects.log: You were awake. You let the snake think you slept. It is the first secret the tortoise has ever kept, and it is a kind one.

choices.text: Thank it, in the morning

effects.log: The snake says it does not know what you mean. Then, after a long time: "It was a small otter." It was a large otter.

events.text: Another quarrel, about nothing, which is the worst kind. The tortoise wants to stay under the bank; the snake wants to go and look at the new weir the villagers built. It goes on for days. You lie on the bottom with both heads out, facing opposite ways, like a gate bolt carved by someone in a bad mood.

choices.text: The tortoise wins: stay

effects.log: You stay. The snake sulks for a month, very quietly, round your shell. The weir is still there when it stops sulking.

choices.text: The snake wins: go and look

effects.log: You go and look. It is a weir. The tortoise says nothing about it for a month, very pointedly.

choices.text: Play stones for it on the riverbed

ok.log: Black pebbles and white on a flat stone. The snake cheats; the tortoise lets it; the snake wins and then, out of shame, suggests the bank after all.

fail.log: The current takes the pebbles halfway through. You both laugh, which you did not expect, and forget what the quarrel was.

choices.text: Both heads: go and look at the weir, and come straight back

effects.log: There and back in an evening. The snake sees its weir; the tortoise is home by dark. It is not a clever answer. It is a good one.

events.text: Your first enemy is grey and patient and stands on one leg. Every morning the heron walks the shallows by the black-sand bank, where the eggs hatch, and every morning it eats a little more of the river's young. Today its yellow eye has found you.

choices.text: The tortoise draws in and becomes a pebble

effects.log: Head in, legs in, the snake pulled in flat against the shell. The beak taps you once, hard, and the heron moves on. A pebble is not food. You will be a pebble a great deal in your life.

choices.text: The snake strikes at the yellow foot

effects.log: The snake bites a heron's toe. It is like biting a reed. The heron jumps, more surprised than hurt, and flaps off to stand somewhere less strange. (-5 health)

choices.text: Run for the deep water

ok.log: The tortoise runs, which is not fast, while the snake watches the beak and says now, now, left. You reach the deep water a breath ahead of it.

fail.log: The beak takes you out of the water and drops you on the stones. You land on your back. It takes a terrible minute to turn over, and the heron, luckily, is distracted by a fish. (-10 health)

events.text: The heron again, a year older and no less patient. This time it does not peck. It picks you up whole and stands there with you in its beak, deciding. The shell holds. The shell is very good at holding. The snake, wound round the outside of the shell, is not inside anything.

choices.text: The tortoise holds shut and lets the snake fend for itself

effects.log: The shell holds. The beak finds the snake instead and pinches it until the heron gets bored and drops you. The snake is torn and silent for a month. The tortoise knows exactly what it did. (-8 health)

choices.text: The snake strikes for the heron's eye

ok.log: The snake goes for the eye and gets the edge of it. The heron drops you in the river and goes off shaking its head, and never troubles your stretch of water again.

fail.log: The snake strikes and misses, and the heron shakes you like a wet rag until you fall. You land in the reeds, sore in two bodies. (-12 health)

choices.text: Both heads: the tortoise opens just enough to pull the snake inside

effects.log: There is room in a shell for a snake if the tortoise gives up some of its own. It does. Both heads inside, the heron finds nothing to pinch and drops a stone back in the river. Inside, in the dark, the snake is very quiet against the tortoise's neck.

events.text: The heron is old. It stands in the same shallows in the frost, feathers ragged, not fishing. You are as wide as its foot is long now, and it looks at you the way old enemies look, as if you were the only one left who remembers it young.

choices.text: The tortoise lets it be

effects.log: You graze past it every morning until the snow. In spring it is gone. The tortoise finds it misses the heron, and is surprised, and does not tell the snake.

choices.text: The snake goes and bites its old toe, once, for luck

effects.log: The snake bites the old toe, gently, and the heron looks down at it with something like approval. Then it flies away up the river for the last time.

events.text: The end of the tenth month. The other turtles of the river stop coming up to bask; one by one they dig into the mud under the bank. The edges of the river freeze in the night, thin as paper, and in the morning the paper is thicker. Something old in the tortoise says: go down. Something old in the snake says: go down, and do not come up.

choices.text: The tortoise picks the place: deep mud under the bank, where the old turtles go

effects.log: You dig in beside two old turtles who do not look at you. The mud is cold and black and smells of last year. It is right. The tortoise knows it is right.

choices.text: The snake picks the place: a crack under a sunken log, out of the current

effects.log: The snake finds a crack under a log that nobody else has found. It is a little warmer, and a little more dangerous. You wedge in.

choices.text: Stay up as long as you can, to see the ice come

effects.log: You watch the ice close over the river from below, like a lid going on, white and then grey and then dark. It is the most beautiful thing either head has ever seen, and you nearly leave it too late.

events.text: Deep winter. The tortoise's heart beats once in a long while, slow as a dripping eave. But the snake was not made for this. A snake goes still in the cold and grows stiller, and stiller, and the snake round your shell has stopped moving altogether. Its head lies against your neck like a cold twig.

choices.text: The tortoise keeps it close and does not sleep

effects.log: All winter the tortoise keeps its neck against the snake's head and does not let itself go deep. It is the longest winter of its life. In the dark, very faintly, the snake's tongue flickers once against your throat. (-6 health)

choices.text: Trust the snake. It knows how to be cold

ok.log: The snake is not dead. It is doing what snakes do, which looks like dying. The tortoise sleeps, afraid, and wakes in the thaw with the snake already awake and laughing at it.

fail.log: The cold goes too deep. In the thaw the snake does not move for nine days, and on the tenth it moves, barely. It is never quite as quick in the cold again. (-15 health)

events.text: The long dark. No sun, no sound but the river going over the ice above, no hunger, no time. The two of you lie in the mud and talk, very slowly, the way you can only talk under ice: one word now, the answer a day later.

choices.text: The tortoise tells the snake about patience

effects.log: It takes the tortoise the whole winter to explain patience. The snake says, at the end, that it understood in the first week and was being patient. The tortoise is so pleased it nearly wakes up.

choices.text: The snake tells the tortoise about the stars

effects.log: The snake counted stars through the water all autumn. Seven of them in the north, it says, in the shape of a dipper, and seven more like a turtle. The tortoise does not believe it. It is true.

choices.text: Say nothing, and dream the same dream

effects.log: For one night in the middle of the winter, two heads dream one dream: a black wall, painted, with a tortoise and a snake on it, facing each other. Neither of you mentions it in the spring.

events.text: The first thaw. A crack runs across the ice above you with a sound like a whip, then another, and grey light comes down through the water, and the river begins to move. You have lived through your first winter under the ice. Both of you. The tortoise lifts its head. The snake is already looking up.

choices.text: Climb out into the first sun on the black sand

effects.log: The black sand drinks the spring sun and gives it back. You lie on it until you are warm all through, two heads in the light, the first winter behind you.

choices.text: The snake goes hunting at once: it is starving

effects.log: The snake takes two tadpoles and a beetle before the tortoise has finished yawning. The belly is full by noon. The tortoise had been meaning to mention it was hungry.

choices.text: The tortoise stays down one more day, to be sure

effects.log: One more day in the mud while the ice breaks up overhead. An ice floe the size of a door scrapes over the place where you would have been. The snake says, grudgingly, that one more day was right.

events.text: Another winter coming, and you know the way now. Down under the bank, into the mud. But this year the snake does not go stiff and frightened at the first frost. It winds itself tight round the shell, head against the tortoise's neck, and says: "Wake me when it is over. You always do."

choices.text: Promise

effects.log: The tortoise promises. It keeps the promise every winter for the rest of your life, and there will be a very great many winters.

choices.text: Say: wake yourself. You are not a child

effects.log: The snake does not answer. In the spring it wakes itself, early, and is out of the mud before the tortoise. It does not mention it. It does not need to.

events.text: Children at the ford in summer, the way there always are: shrieking, splashing, turning over stones for crayfish. Then a hand comes down out of the sky and closes round you, and you are in the air, and a face as big as the moon is looking at you. "A turtle," says {npc}. "With a snake on it. Look. Look!" Six more faces come to look.

choices.text: The tortoise draws in and waits it out

effects.log: You are passed from hand to hand, shaken, held up to the sun, put down on a stone and picked up again. You stay shut through all of it. In the end the children get bored and go back to crayfish, and {npc} sets you down in the water very carefully, as if you might break.

choices.text: The snake rears up and hisses at the moon-faces

effects.log: Six children scream and run. {npc} does not. {npc} holds you closer to {his} face, delighted, and says, "It talks!"

choices.text: Both heads come out and look back at {him}

effects.log: Two heads look at one child. {npc} goes completely quiet, the way children go quiet in a shrine, and then whispers, "Hello," to each head in turn, and puts you back exactly where you were.

events.text: {npc} has come back to the ford with a stick of charcoal from the kitchen fire and a cracked inkstone and a terrible idea. You are on a flat stone in the sun. {npc} is going to write on your shell, the way the village schoolmaster writes on paper, because {he} has just learned three characters and wants something to keep them on.

choices.text: Let {him}. The tortoise holds very still

effects.log: The brush tickles. {npc} writes long, and life, and a third character that might be water and might be a mistake. They wash off in a week. Something about being written on stays with the tortoise much longer.

choices.text: The snake reads over {his} shoulder, so to speak

effects.log: The snake watches every stroke of the brush and learns the three shapes before the soot is dry. Long. Life. Water, probably. They are the first characters it ever learns. It will learn a great many more.

choices.text: Crawl away before the soot is dry

effects.log: You go off the stone with half a character on your back. {npc} chases you into the river with the brush, laughing. The half character stays a long time, and the other turtles look at it.

events.text: The bigger children at the ford have found you again, without {npc}, and this time they have a jar. A big child with a scabbed knee holds you over it and says turtles fetch a coin at the medicine shop. {npc} comes running down the bank, too late, shouting. The big child's thumb is right next to the snake's head.

choices.text: The snake bites the thumb

effects.log: The snake bites. The big child howls and drops you, and you are in the river before the jar is turned over. {npc} laughs so hard {he} sits down in the shallows. The thumb is fine. Its owner's opinion of turtles is not.

choices.text: The snake does not bite. The tortoise holds shut

effects.log: You go into the jar. Then {npc} arrives, and there is shouting, and a shove, and the jar goes over, and you go back into the river with a great deal of other water. The snake is very proud of not biting. It mentions it for a year.

choices.text: Both heads: the snake hisses but does not bite, and the tortoise kicks

effects.log: A hiss in the big child's face and four kicking legs at once. The big child drops you from pure astonishment. Nobody is bitten. {npc} tells the whole village about it for a week.

events.text: A young person comes down to the ford with a bundle on {his} back and a pair of new straw sandals, leaving the village for good. It is {npc}, grown. {He} sits on the flat stone where {he} once wrote on a turtle, and looks at the water, and says to nobody: "Long life. I never learned the third one properly."

choices.text: Come up onto the stone beside {him}

effects.log: {npc} sees you and laughs out loud, alone at the ford. "You," {he} says. "Both of you." {He} touches your shell once, where the characters were, and goes off up the road a great deal lighter.

choices.text: Stay under the water and watch {him} go

effects.log: You watch from under the water until the sandals are out of sight. The snake says it was water, the third character. The tortoise says it does not matter now. It is the saddest thing the tortoise has ever said.

events.text: A net in the shallows, a hand, the dark of a basket. {npc}, a turtle-peddler with a pole across {his} shoulders, has been along the river all morning taking every small turtle {he} can find. There are thirty of you in the basket, climbing on each other in the dark, and every one of them is frightened, and only one of them has two heads. Tomorrow is market day.

choices.text: The tortoise goes to the bottom of the basket and waits

effects.log: At the bottom it is dark and quiet and other turtles stand on you. The tortoise lets them. Whatever happens at the market will happen; you will be there for it.

choices.text: The snake works at the weave of the basket all night

ok.log: By dawn the snake has worked a hole in the weave big enough for a turtle. Not for you, it turns out, with a snake round you. But six other turtles go out through it into the river while the peddler sleeps. The snake is unreasonably pleased.

fail.log: The weave is tight and the snake's teeth are small. By dawn there is a frayed place and nothing else. The peddler shoulders the pole and you go up the road to market, swinging.

choices.text: Both heads keep the other turtles calm

effects.log: The tortoise is still and the snake is watchful, and somehow the stillness spreads through the basket. By midnight thirty turtles are lying quiet in the dark, and the peddler, who has carried a great many baskets, says it is the calmest load {he} has ever had.

events.text: Market day, the fifth of the month. Salt, straw sandals, dried fish, a man selling knives, and on the next mat a fortune-teller, {npc}, with a little brazier and a stack of old turtle plastrons, brown and cracked. {npc} looks into the peddler's basket and goes very still, and points at you. "That one. How much for the one with two heads?"

choices.text: The tortoise shuts up tight and looks like nothing

effects.log: You become the most ordinary turtle in the world. The fortune-teller frowns, reaches in, and picks up the turtle next to you by mistake, and pays for it, and is very angry later.

choices.text: The snake hisses at the fortune-teller

effects.log: {npc} jerks back. "A snake on it," {he} says to the peddler. "Bad luck. Bad luck for a fortune-teller." {He} does not buy you. {He} watches you the rest of the morning over the top of {his} brazier.

choices.text: Both heads look straight at {npc}

effects.log: Two heads look at the fortune-teller, and the fortune-teller looks back, and something passes between you that is very like recognition. {npc} sits down again without buying. "Not yet," {he} says quietly, to nobody. "Not this one. Not yet."

events.text: Late in the day a child comes to the peddler's mat with a string of copper coins: festival coins, the ones the old people give at the New Year, saved. {npc} is perhaps eight. {He} wants to buy a turtle to let go at the temple for a grandmother who is sick, because the monk said a life set free is good for a life that is ending. {He} looks into the basket for a long time.

choices.text: The tortoise lifts its head to be seen

mem.note: chose me, the turtle with two heads

effects.log: The tortoise lifts its head out of the crowd of shells and waits. {npc} sees it and says, "That one." The peddler laughs and says the snake costs extra. It does not. {npc} pays with every coin {he} has.

choices.text: The snake climbs to the top of the basket

mem.note: chose me, the turtle with two heads

effects.log: The snake hauls you up over three other turtles to the top of the pile and stares at the child. {npc} is not afraid of it at all. "That one," {he} says. "It wants to go."

choices.text: Stay in the crowd and let the child choose

mem.note: let me choose you, the turtle with two heads

effects.log: {npc} picks you anyway, out of thirty, and says {he} does not know why. Children choose the strange one; it is how the strange ones live.

events.text: The walk to the temple, in a gourd dipper of water, in two small hands. Up the valley road, past the stone guardian posts, through the gate with the four fierce kings painted on its walls, to a pond under a pine where lotus leaves lie flat on the water. A monk says a few words of the sutra. {npc} holds the dipper over the pond, and says the grandmother's name, and lets go.

choices.text: Go down into the pond slowly, and look back once

effects.log: The water is green and warm and smells of incense from the hall. You look back once. {npc} is still on the bank with the empty dipper, looking at the place you went in. You are a temple turtle now.

choices.text: The snake goes down fast, before anyone changes their mind

effects.log: Into the water and under a lotus leaf in one quick twist. The snake has heard that released turtles are sometimes caught again and sold again. It is taking no chances.

choices.text: Both heads stay at the edge until the child has gone

effects.log: You stay at the edge of the pond with both heads out until {npc} has walked down through the gate. The child turns at the gate and bows, very seriously, to a turtle. The grandmother lives another eleven years.

events.text: The eighth day of the fourth month: the Buddha's Birthday. Lanterns of five colours along the temple paths, and the whole valley come up to make merit. And {npc}, grown now, comes to the pond with a basket and an old monk and a plan. The temple pond is full, the monk says; the old turtles should go to the river, to be truly free. {npc} kneels at the edge and finds you at once. Of course {he} does. There is only one with two heads.

choices.text: Go into the basket. The river is the road

mem.note: went into the river when I let you go

effects.log: Down the valley to the river, the lanterns behind you. {npc} wades in to the knees and opens the basket, and you go out into cold moving open water for the first time since you were a coin. The pond is up the stream you can see from here. You know the way back. You do not need it yet.

choices.text: The snake slips the basket on the path and finds its own way down

ok.log: Out through the basket's weave, down the bank, along a field ditch to the river, alone, while {npc} hunts the path for you. The snake wanted to arrive free, not carried. You reach open water by moonlight.

fail.log: The snake gets you out of the basket and straight into a ditch with no water in it. {npc} finds you there, laughing, and carries you the rest of the way in both hands. The tortoise does not say anything. It does not need to.

choices.text: Stay in the pond. Not yet

effects.log: You go down under the lotus roots where no hand can reach. {npc} looks for a long time and goes away with the other turtles. The snake asks the tortoise what it is waiting for. The tortoise does not know. It knows how to wait.

events.text: The child with the coins looks into the basket, and for a moment you are somewhere else. Night, drums, a village well, and a face looking down into it out of a turtle made of sorghum leaves, dropping a rice cake into the dark. It is this child's face. It is not this child at all. The snake tastes the air and says, very quietly: "We have met this one before. Or you have."

choices.text: The tortoise lets the feeling be, and waits to be chosen

effects.log: You do not understand it, and you do not need to. Some debts are older than the one who owes them. The child chooses you, as you knew {he} would.

choices.text: The snake tries to work out what it means

effects.log: The snake turns the memory over and over and gets nowhere. A rice cake, a well, a face. It decides it will understand it one day. It is right, though the day is very far off.

events.text: Market day at the ford, and you are in a bucket on a mat, waiting to be bought, next to the fortune-teller {npc}. A farmer wants to know whether to plant early. {npc} takes a turtle's under-shell, old and brown, drilled on the back with rows of little hollows, and holds a red-hot iron rod into one hollow until the shell goes POK, and a crack runs across the front in the shape of a little branch.

choices.text: The snake watches the crack and learns its shape

effects.log: The crack goes across and then down. {npc} says: plant late. The snake memorises the crack like a word. It will watch every crack at every market for the rest of its life.

choices.text: The tortoise watches the shell, and understands what it is

effects.log: It is a turtle's belly. Somebody's. It was alive in a river once, and now it is a thing that goes POK. The tortoise draws its own belly in close against the bottom of the bucket and does not sleep that night.

events.text: {npc} is reading cracks for a woman whose son has gone to the coast for work. The crack comes out crooked. {npc} looks at it, and you see {him} decide, before {he} speaks, to say it is a good crack. The woman weeps with relief and pays double. The snake, which has been studying cracks for a season now, can read that it was a bad one.

choices.text: The snake admires the lie

effects.log: A crack says what it says. A fortune-teller says what the paying one needs. The snake thinks this is the cleverest thing it has seen on land. The tortoise thinks it is the saddest.

choices.text: The tortoise wants to know what the crack really said

effects.log: You never find out. The woman never comes back to the market. The tortoise thinks about that mother for years, which is the start of something it does not yet have a name for: wanting to know how things end.

choices.text: Both heads: a true reading and a kind one are two different things

effects.log: The snake reads; the tortoise remembers. Between the two of you, you understand that there are two kinds of telling: what was seen, and what was meant. You will have to choose between them on your own back one day.

events.text: Evening, the market packing up. {npc} looks into your bucket and turns you over with one finger and looks at your belly-shell for a long time. "Too young," {he} says. "Come back in a hundred years." And {he} tips the bucket into the river on the way home, all of you, because {he} cannot be bothered to carry it.

choices.text: The tortoise remembers the face

effects.log: The tortoise remembers that face, and the brazier, and the word hundred. The river closes over you. A hundred years is not so long, for a tortoise.

choices.text: The snake bites the finger on the way out

effects.log: A quick bite in passing. {npc} swears and shakes the finger and laughs. "Two hundred years, then," {he} calls after you into the dark water. "I will tell my grandchildren."

events.text: Every morning after the dawn chant, an old monk comes down to the pond with a wooden fish, the hollow drum carved like a fish with its eyes always open, and taps it, and chants over the released turtles. There are nineteen turtles in the pond. The monk knows each of them, and gives each a name from the sutras, and has now, after some thought, given you two.

choices.text: The tortoise comes to the edge every morning to listen

effects.log: The chant goes on and on and does not hurry, and the tortoise likes it better than anything it has ever heard. The monk notices which turtle comes every morning, and smiles.

choices.text: The snake listens for the words, not the sound

effects.log: The snake learns the chant the way it learned the three characters at the ford: whole, by heart, without meaning to. By autumn it can hiss the first line. The monk would be horrified, or delighted.

choices.text: Stay under the lotus. A pond is only a bigger basket

effects.log: You stay under the lotus roots all summer, and listen anyway, because sound goes through water. You do not want to like this place. You like it a little.

events.text: The lotus opens in the seventh month, all at once, pink and white, the pads as wide as a tray. You sit on one in the morning sun with a dragonfly on your shell and two heads out, and the pilgrims coming up the path stop and point and press their palms together, and a woman with a baby on her back throws a coin into the pond for luck. It hits the snake.

choices.text: The tortoise sits on and lets them look

effects.log: You sit through the whole festival on the lotus pad. People come from three villages to see the turtle with two heads in the temple pond. The monk says nothing, and the coins in the pond pay for a new roof.

choices.text: The snake throws the coin back, more or less

effects.log: The snake noses the coin to the edge of the pad and flicks it, and it falls back into the pond with a plop. The pilgrims shriek with laughter. A rumour goes round the valley that the temple turtle refuses money.

events.text: The monk sits by the pond in the evening and explains to the turtles, as if to novices, that a creature set free for merit carries the vow of the one who set it free. The child who brought you made a vow for a grandmother. You did not make it. You find that you are keeping it anyway: you do not leave the pond, and the grandmother does not die.

choices.text: Keep the vow you did not make

effects.log: A year, another year. It is not a chain. Nobody would stop you. You stay because a child gave every coin there was, and that is worth something even to a turtle. The tortoise understands, for the first time, what it is to keep a word.

choices.text: The snake says a vow it did not make is not its vow

effects.log: "Not ours," says the snake. The tortoise does not argue. But it does not go to the outflow either, and the snake, after a while, stops looking at it.

choices.text: Both heads keep it, for different reasons

effects.log: The tortoise keeps it because a vow is a vow. The snake keeps it because it wants to see whether the grandmother really lives. Both reasons are good. Between them they hold.

events.text: Before dawn the bell in the pavilion is struck, and the sound goes down into the pond and through the water and into your shell, and stays there humming long after the last stroke. This morning the old monk does not come down after the chant. A young monk comes instead, with the wooden fish, and taps it badly, and does not know your names.

choices.text: Come to the edge for the young monk anyway

effects.log: The young monk sees one turtle come to the edge, alone, and is so moved that the mallet slips into the pond. You bring it back up on your shell. It becomes a story at that temple for generations.

choices.text: Go to the hall at night, where they have laid the old monk out

effects.log: Up the steps and along the cold boards at midnight, to the room with the lamp and the body under hemp. You stay by the door until the monks come for the morning rites. It is the first ending you ever go to see on purpose. It will not be the last.

events.text: A pilgrim kneels at the pond's edge to release a turtle bought at the market, and says the words wrong, and lowers it into the water with both hands, slowly, the way the temple people do. Something in the way the hands open makes you remember: a sorghum turtle, a well, a real turtle lifted out and carried down to the river at night. Your own hands. You never had hands.

choices.text: The tortoise keeps the memory and asks nothing of it

effects.log: Somebody once carried a turtle to the river for merit. Somebody was you. The tortoise lets the memory lie in the bottom of its mind like a coin in a pond.

choices.text: The snake swims to meet the new turtle

effects.log: The snake shows the new turtle where the warm stones are, and the lotus roots, and the place where no hand can reach. You were carried once. It seems only fair.

events.text: The biggest thing in the pond is a carp, gold gone pale, whiskers like an old scholar's, released here forty years ago by a magistrate's widow. It has a voice like bubbles and an opinion about everything. It tells you, on your first evening, that it is not really a pond carp. It is a courtier of the Dragon King's palace under the sea, caught by mistake.

choices.text: The tortoise listens to all of it

effects.log: Coral gates, a hall of pearls, a king with a beard of weed, fish ministers in hats. The carp talks until the stars come out. Half of it must be true. The tortoise does not mind which half.

choices.text: The snake asks it sharp questions

effects.log: What colour are the gates. How many ministers. Who carries the king's letters to the rivers. The carp answers every question without a pause, and the snake decides it is either telling the truth or the best liar in the world, and respects it either way.

events.text: The carp explains, one autumn, who carries the Dragon King's letters to the rivers. Turtles. Old ones, very old, in small black hats, with a kelp scroll under one flipper. "You have the look of an envoy," it says. "Both of you. One to carry the letter and one to read it first."

choices.text: The tortoise wants to carry letters

effects.log: To carry a word across a sea for someone, and give it into the right hands. The tortoise thinks about it all winter. It has never wanted anything so much.

choices.text: The snake wants to read them

effects.log: The snake does not say so, but it would very much like to read the Dragon King's letters. All of them. Before anyone else.

choices.text: Both heads: one to carry and one to read, as the carp said

effects.log: You look at each other, which is hard to do when one of you is wound round the other. The carp is right, which you will never tell it. A carrier and a reader. A word kept and a word understood.

events.text: The carp is dying. It hangs in the deep end of the pond, slow, its gold gone grey, and asks you for one thing. Its scale, when it is dead, carried to the sea, to the Dragon King's gate, so the king knows one courtier never forgot. "It is a long way," it says. "You have a long time."

choices.text: The tortoise promises

effects.log: The tortoise promises, and takes the great pale scale under its shell when the carp has gone still, and keeps it there. The sea is a long way. You have a long time. A word, kept, before you even know that keeping words is what you are for.

choices.text: The snake asks what the Dragon King would give for it

effects.log: The carp laughs, bubbles all the way up. "Everything," it says, "and nothing." The snake takes the scale. It is not sure, yet, which of those it is taking it for.

choices.text: Stay with it till the end, and do not promise

effects.log: You stay beside it in the deep end all night. It talks about coral and pearls until it stops. In the morning the monks net it out and bury it under the pine. You did not promise. The tortoise wishes it had.

events.text: A carpenter is mending the temple gate. The old bolt-holders have split, and the new ones, the carpenter tells the novice who is holding the chisels, will be turtles: a pair of them, facing each other, so the bolt slides through both their shells. "For long life," the carpenter says. "And so nothing bad comes in. Turtles are stubborn." To get the shape right, the carpenter goes down to the pond to look at a real one.

choices.text: Climb out onto the warm step and sit for the carving

effects.log: You sit on the step all afternoon in the sun while the chisel goes, and the shavings fall, and the carpenter keeps glancing at you, and once, kindly, moves you into the shade.

choices.text: Stay in the pond and let the carpenter guess

effects.log: The carpenter watches the pond for an hour, sees nothing but a ripple, and carves turtles out of memory and a story. They come out looking surprised. They are very good turtles anyway.

events.text: The new bolt-holders are on the gate: two turtles carved in pine, facing each other, the long bolt through both. The carpenter has looked at you, and has carved what was there: one tortoise, and then, because the gate needs a pair, the same tortoise again, facing itself. There is no snake. Not on either of them. The snake looks at the gate for a long time.

choices.text: The snake is offended, and says so

effects.log: The snake hisses at the gate every evening for a month. Two tortoises facing each other, and nobody to finish their sentences. The tortoise says it is only a gate. The snake says that is exactly what it is worried about.

choices.text: The tortoise sees itself split in two, and is afraid

effects.log: Two of you, facing each other, and the bolt between. The tortoise looks at it and thinks: that is what we would be, without the snake. Two halves of a lock, staring. It goes down into the pond and stays close to the snake all night.

choices.text: Both heads: we will be on a wall one day, the right way

effects.log: You do not know where the thought comes from. A wall, a dark one, painted. A tortoise and a snake, wound round each other, the heads turned face to face. One creature. You both have the thought at once, and neither of you mentions it.

events.text: A winter night, the gate barred. Something tries to come in: a fox, or a thief, or something that is neither, and the bolt holds, and the two pine turtles hold it. In the morning there are scratches all round the gate and none on the turtles. The novices say the turtles held the gate. The snake, who heard the whole thing from the pond, says they were only wood.

choices.text: The tortoise says wood can be stubborn too

effects.log: Something that waits, and does not move, and is there in the morning. The tortoise feels a strange kinship with two pieces of pine. It spends the winter close to the gate wall of the pond.

choices.text: The snake admits, privately, that they did well

effects.log: The snake goes up the bank in the night and looks at the gate for a long time, and then, very quietly, tells the two pine turtles that they did well. The tortoise pretends to be asleep.

events.text: Every evening at dusk an old woman comes up the temple path, {npc}, and sits on the flat stone by the pond, and talks to it. Not to the monks, not to the Buddha in the hall. To the pond. A son gone for a soldier, a daughter-in-law with a temper, a hip that aches when the wind is from the east. {He} does not seem to expect an answer. {He} has been doing it for a year before you notice that you are the only one listening.
events.arc: The Woman Who Talks to the Pond

choices.text: The tortoise comes to the stone every evening

mem.note: listened to me from the pond

effects.log: You come to the edge of the stone and put your head out and stay. {npc} sees you on the third evening and stops talking. Then {he} goes on, to you now. It is a different kind of talking, when someone is there.

choices.text: The snake listens from under the lotus and remembers everything

effects.log: The son's name, the soldier's camp, the daughter-in-law's village, the hip. The snake stores all of it away the way it stores characters and cracks. It does not know yet what it is keeping it for.

choices.text: Both heads come out onto the stone beside {him}

mem.note: sat with me, both heads at once

effects.log: {npc} looks at the two heads beside {him} on the stone and laughs, the first time in a long time. "Two of you," {he} says. "Good. One to listen and one to remember."

events.text: {npc} brings a rice ball one evening and breaks it into the water, a grain at a time, and tells you that the son has written: the first letter in three years, carried by a salt merchant, read aloud by the village schoolmaster. The boy is alive. The boy is coming home in the autumn. {npc} has told nobody else yet. {He} wanted to tell the pond first.
events.arc: The Woman Who Talks to the Pond

choices.text: The tortoise eats the rice, slowly, a grain at a time

effects.log: One grain, and a pause, and one grain. {npc} watches you eat every one of them and tells the letter again, from the beginning. You listen to it twice. You would listen to it ten times.

choices.text: The snake wants to know what else the letter said

effects.log: There is a line the schoolmaster stumbled over and {npc} did not understand. The snake turns it over all night. It suspects the boy owes someone money. It is right. It keeps it to itself, which is, for the snake, a kind of tenderness.

events.text: The son did not come home in the autumn. Or the next. {npc} still comes every evening, slower on the path now, and sits on the stone, and some evenings says nothing at all for an hour. Tonight {he} says: "If the boy comes and I am gone, you tell the boy. Say the one who bore that child waited. Say I was not angry." Then {he} laughs at {him}self, asking a turtle.
events.arc: The Woman Who Talks to the Pond

choices.text: The tortoise puts its head against {his} hand: a promise

effects.log: You cannot speak. You will not be able to for a hundred years. But the tortoise puts its head against the old hand on the stone, and holds it there, and {npc} goes very quiet. A word given to a turtle. You will carry it.

choices.text: The snake remembers the exact words

effects.log: The one who bore that child waited. I was not angry. The snake files the words away exactly, every one, in the place where it keeps the three characters and the shape of the cracks. A word is a thing you can keep. It had not known that.

choices.text: Both heads: one holds the promise, one holds the words

mem.note: took my word for my son

effects.log: The tortoise takes the promise and the snake takes the words, and between you there is a word kept whole. {npc} cannot know that. {He} goes down the path lighter all the same.

events.text: Years of evenings. Tonight {npc} does not come up the path. Tomorrow neither. On the third day the monks go down to the village, and come back, and one of them sits on the flat stone for a while where {npc} used to sit, and does not know what to say to a pond.
events.arc: The Woman Who Talks to the Pond

choices.text: Go down the valley to the house, to be there for the funeral

ok.npcPass: old age, at home, after twenty years of evenings at the temple pond
ok.log: Down the stream, along a ditch, under a hedge, to a yard full of white hemp and a bier with paper flowers. You lie by the well all through the rites and nobody sees you. The tortoise watches every part of it. It wants to remember exactly how this ended.

fail.npcPass: old age, at home, after twenty years of evenings at the temple pond
fail.log: A dog finds you in the ditch and you lose a day hiding. By the time you reach the yard the bier has gone up the hill. You were not there. The tortoise minds this more than any wound. (-8 health)

choices.text: Stay on the stone, every evening, at dusk, as {he} did

effects.npcPass: old age, at home, after twenty years of evenings at the temple pond
effects.log: Every evening for a year you climb up onto the flat stone at dusk and stay there. The monks begin to call it the old woman's stone. You still have the word for the son. You are keeping it.

events.text: {npc} hums at the pond one evening, half to {him}self, the old children's chant: turtle, turtle, put forth your head. And both your heads come up out of the water at once, before you can stop them, and you are somewhere else: a Chuseok night, a well, a voice chanting the same words down into the dark at a turtle, in a mouth that was yours.
events.arc: The Woman Who Talks to the Pond

choices.text: The tortoise puts its head out further, for {him}

effects.log: {npc} laughs with delight. "Which one came first?" {he} asks. "Did you see? Which one?" You do not know. You think that was always the question.

choices.text: The snake hisses the next line of the chant back

effects.log: Or we will roast you and eat you. The snake hisses it, or something like it, and {npc} nearly falls off the stone, and then laughs until {he} cries. A turtle who knows the chant. Nobody in the village will believe it.

events.text: An otter has found the temple pond. It comes up the stream from the river at night and goes through the pond like a fox through a henhouse: two of the old turtles gone in a week, turned over on the bank and opened. It is quick and clever and it has learned that a shell is only a box, if you know how to hold it.

choices.text: The tortoise goes deep under the lotus roots and stays

effects.log: Three nights under the roots in the black mud, shut. The otter comes and noses and goes. The snake hates every moment of it, and says so, at length, afterwards.

choices.text: The snake goes out to look at it

ok.log: The snake watches it from the reeds for a night and learns it: in by the outflow, round the east side, out by the step before dawn. Every night the same. A clever animal with a habit is half caught.

fail.log: The otter sees the snake first, and comes for it, and gets the shell instead, and turns you over on the bank. You get back into the water on the second try. (-10 health)

events.text: The otter comes up the outflow tonight, as every night, and this time it comes straight for the lotus where you sleep. The snake has been waiting for this for a month. The snake's first real fight.

choices.text: Let the snake fight it

ok.log: The snake strikes for the face, again and again, small and black and furious, while the tortoise braces on the bottom and does not let itself be turned. The otter leaves with a bitten nose and does not come back. The snake shakes for an hour afterwards.

fail.log: The otter is bigger and faster and has done this before. It turns you over twice before a monk with a lantern comes down to see what the noise is. You live, torn, for the lantern. (-30 health)
fail.deathCause: an otter in the temple pond, in the dark

choices.text: The tortoise shuts tight, snake and all, and waits it out

effects.log: The otter turns the shell, worries it, carries it to the bank, gives up near dawn. The snake was inside the whole time, pressed flat, wanting to fight. It does not speak to the tortoise for a week. (-6 health)

choices.text: Both heads: the tortoise braces and the snake strikes from under the rim

effects.log: The tortoise braces low on a root so the otter cannot turn you; the snake strikes out from under the edge of the shell, where the otter is not looking. It takes three strikes. The otter goes back down the outflow and tells every otter on the river.

events.text: A year on, and there are otter tracks again on the bank by the outflow: smaller ones, and the old ones with them. The otter has a family now. The kits play in the stream below the temple and slide down the mud bank in the evening, and never come up into the pond.

choices.text: Let them be. They stay out of the pond

effects.log: You watch them sliding down the bank in the evenings from the edge of the outflow. They watch you back. An arrangement. Most peace is only that.

choices.text: The snake goes down once and shows itself to the kits

effects.log: One small black head rises out of the stream among the kits, and hisses, once. The kits scatter up the bank. The otters never come up the outflow again, any of them, for three generations.

events.text: A grass snake suns itself on the bank above the pond, long and green-gold and free. It has no shell to carry. It goes where it likes, eats when it likes, sleeps in the wall of the bell pavilion. It looks down at your snake, wound round its tortoise like a rope round a jar, and laughs.

choices.text: The snake ignores it

effects.log: The snake looks at the grass snake once, and then away, and is very busy with a snail for the rest of the afternoon. The tortoise notices how busy.

choices.text: The snake goes up the bank to talk to it

effects.log: You go up the bank, because there is no other way for the snake to go. The two snakes talk in the grass, very quietly, and the tortoise lies in the sun between them and hears all of it.

events.text: The grass snake comes back every day now, and talks. The walls of the old shrine in the hills, it says, are full of mice. The fields in summer go on for ever. And a snake can uncoil. Did yours know that? Any snake can. One turn, and then another. It does not hurt. It only takes deciding.

choices.text: The tortoise says nothing, and listens to the snake listening

effects.log: The tortoise does not argue, or beg, or draw in. It lies there and listens to its own snake listening to the grass snake, which is the hardest thing it has ever done.

choices.text: The tortoise turns and walks back into the pond, snake and all

effects.log: Into the water, away from the voice. The snake comes too, because it must. It does not forgive the tortoise for deciding, all that summer.

choices.text: The snake asks the grass snake what it is like to be alone

effects.log: The grass snake thinks about it for a long time. "Quiet," it says, at last. "Very quiet." Your snake does not answer. The tortoise has never been so glad of a silence.

events.text: Night, and the snake has made up its mind to try. Not to go. Only to see. It unwinds one turn from round the shell, slowly, and lies with its head on the bank, half free. The tortoise feels the place where it was go cold.

choices.text: The snake winds itself back on, of its own accord

effects.log: It lies there half free until the moon moves. Then, without a word, it winds the turn back on, tighter than before. It never explains. The tortoise never asks. But in the morning the grass snake is gone, and so is something you did not know was there between you: a door left open.

choices.text: The tortoise speaks first: stay

effects.log: The tortoise says one word. It is not a command. It is not even a request. It is just the truth, said aloud. The snake winds back on. The word sits between you for a hundred years, and is never said again, because it does not need to be.

choices.text: The snake goes up the bank for one night

ok.log: It uncoils almost all the way, and stretches out in the grass, and for one night it is nearly a free snake with a turtle on the end of its tail. At dawn it comes back. "Quiet," it says. "Very quiet." It does not try again.

fail.log: It uncoils too far, and a fox finds the long thin thing in the grass, and you are both in its mouth before the snake can wind back. The fox drops you at the edge of the pond. The snake winds on so tight the tortoise cannot breathe, and neither of you speaks for a season. (-12 health)

events.text: Long after, a hot afternoon, the bank empty. The tortoise says, without warning, after years of saying nothing about it: "I heard you. That night. I heard you think about it." The snake goes very still round the shell.

choices.text: The snake says: and I came back

effects.log: "And I came back," says the snake. That is all it says. It is enough, or it will have to be. The tortoise draws its head in, and out again, and you lie in the sun together like any turtle.

choices.text: The snake says: I would think it again

effects.log: "I would think it again," says the snake. "I will think it again, some year. You will hear me. And I will come back." The tortoise finds that this is a better promise than a sweet one.

choices.text: Both heads: then we will always say so aloud

effects.log: An agreement, the first you ever make in words: whatever one head thinks of leaving, it will say aloud, and the other will hear it out. It is not a chain. It is the opposite of a chain. It holds better.

events.text: The grass snake comes back, older and fatter, and does not laugh this time. It has had a hard winter. It lies on the warm stone above the pond and says, as if it had been thinking about it for years: "You did not come. I thought you would. Was it worth it, staying wound round a stone?"

choices.text: The snake says yes

effects.log: One word. The grass snake looks at the two of you a long time and goes off into the grass, and the tortoise feels the snake round its shell tighten, very slightly, the way a hand does.

choices.text: The snake shares a frog with it instead of answering

effects.log: The snake takes a frog and leaves half on the stone. The grass snake eats it. Neither of them says anything about staying or going. Old snakes do not need to.

events.text: The Knot is loose this year, and you both feel it. The snake lies half unwound in the mornings, and looks at the bank, and the outflow, and the road. Nobody is tempting it. That is worse. It is tempting itself.

choices.text: Let the heads talk, the whole season

effects.log: A season of talk on the bottom of the pond: old quarrels, old stories, the heron, the first winter under the ice. By autumn the snake is wound tight again, and pretends it never was not.

choices.text: The tortoise grows quiet and waits it out

effects.log: The tortoise waits, the way it waits for winter to end. The snake does not go. But it does not come back closer, either, and the tortoise begins to wonder whether waiting is always the answer.

choices.text: The snake goes off hunting on its own, as far as it can reach

effects.log: As far as a snake can reach with a tortoise on the end of it, which is not far. It eats well. It comes back sulky and full. Something has been decided, by not deciding.

events.text: There are nineteen turtles in the pond and they bask on the same log every afternoon, in a row, all facing the sun. When you climb on at the end, the nearest one shuffles away. Then the next. They are not unkind. They do not know what a turtle with two heads is for, and they would rather not find out.

choices.text: The tortoise sits at the end of the log anyway, every day

effects.log: Every afternoon, at the end of the log, a little gap between you and the rest. After a year the gap is a hand narrower. After two, the old ones have stopped noticing it. That is not the same as closing it.

choices.text: The snake hisses the whole row off the log

effects.log: Splash, splash, splash, nineteen turtles in the water. You have the whole log. It is warm and empty, and the snake is pleased for an hour, and then it is not.

events.text: A grey evening in the rain. The other turtles have dug in together under the bank in a heap of shells, the way they do, warm against each other. There is no room in the heap for a turtle with a snake round it. You lie a little apart in the cold. It is the first time either head has known the word lonely.

choices.text: The tortoise says: we have each other

effects.log: The tortoise says it, and means it, and it is true. The snake says nothing, and winds a little tighter. It is still a cold night.

choices.text: The snake says: we are better than a heap

effects.log: The snake says it, and half believes it. You are not a heap. You are something else, something the pond has no word for. That will be useful one day. Tonight it is only cold.

choices.text: Both heads go and lie against the heap from the outside

effects.log: You lie down against the outside of the heap of shells in the rain. Nobody moves away. In the morning one of the old turtles is lying against your shell instead of the heap, asleep, as if by accident.

events.text: One of the pond turtles does not mind. She is old and half blind and has a notch in her shell from a boat, and she basks beside you every afternoon now, close, and talks to the tortoise about weed and to the snake about frogs, as if it were the most ordinary thing in the world to talk to a turtle in two directions.

choices.text: The tortoise basks beside her every day until she dies

effects.log: Nine summers of afternoons. When she does not come out in the tenth spring, the tortoise goes and lies on the place on the log where she lay, and the snake does not tease it, not once.

choices.text: The snake brings her frogs she cannot catch any more

effects.log: She cannot see well enough to hunt. The snake can. Every few days there is a frog by her on the log. She never asks where they come from. She knows.

events.text: No rain since the fifth month. The pond goes down a hand's width a week. The lotus leaves lie on mud, then on dry mud, then curl. The monks carry water up from the well for the turtles, a bucket at a time, and pray for rain, and the magistrate in the town below has a rain rite at the dragon pool, and nothing comes.

choices.text: The tortoise digs into the last mud and waits for rain

effects.log: Down into the cracked mud at the deep end, shut, waiting, the way a tortoise waits. The mud goes hard around you. The rain does not come. (-5 health)

choices.text: The snake goes up the bank at night to find where the water went

effects.log: The snake tastes the night air for a long time from the top of the bank. Far off, very faint, cold and moving: the river. It is a long way. It is that way.

events.text: The pond is a puddle. The other turtles lie in it in a heap, hardly moving. The monks have stopped bringing water; the well is low too. Tonight the snake says it plainly: stay and bake, or go. The river is three nights away over dry fields, and the tortoise has never walked three nights in its life.

choices.text: Go. The snake finds the way, the tortoise keeps going

effects.log: Up the bank in the dark, over the temple wall by the drain hole, out into the fields. The snake tastes the air and says this way; the tortoise puts one foot down, and the next. It is the first long journey of your life.

choices.text: Stay with the other turtles

effects.log: You stay in the puddle with the heap. On the ninth day the rain comes, all at once, and fills the pond in a night. Two of the old turtles did not live to see it. You did. The snake does not say anything about the river. (-10 health)

choices.text: Take the old notch-shelled turtle with you, pushing her ahead

ok.log: You push her up the bank and through the drain hole. She cannot see where she is going. You can, between you. She comes all the way, slow as you, complaining all the way, alive.

fail.log: She is too heavy and too tired, and at the drain hole she will not go on. She turns back to the puddle. You go on without her, both heads looking back. (-8 health)

events.text: The second night on the dry fields. The rice stands brown and dead in squares, and the ditches are dust, and your throat is dust. The tortoise's legs have stopped hurting, which is worse than hurting. The snake has gone quiet. Somewhere ahead a dog barks at a farmhouse, and the way the snake wants runs right past its gate.

choices.text: The tortoise keeps going, straight past the gate

ok.log: One foot, the next foot. The dog barks itself hoarse at the gate and never thinks to look at the ground. A stone that walks is not a thing dogs know about.

fail.log: The dog finds you and rolls you over in the dust and carries you round the yard until a farmer shouts at it. It drops you in a cabbage row. You go on, slower. (-12 health)

choices.text: The snake finds a longer way round, through the burial mounds

effects.log: Round the long way, between the grass-covered grave mounds of some family on the hill, quiet and dark and dogless. It costs a night. It costs nothing else. (-6 health)

choices.text: Both heads: rest under the dead rice by day, walk only by night

effects.log: The tortoise knows how to stop; the snake knows when it is safe to go. Under the rice stalks in the heat of the day, out under the stars when the dog is asleep. Slower. Safer. Together.

events.text: The third night, and the snake lifts its head and says nothing at all, and the tortoise smells it too: cold, wet, moving. A bank of willows. A slope of grey stones. And then the river, low in the drought but still a river, running black under the moon, going somewhere, going everywhere.

choices.text: Slide down the bank into it

effects.log: Cold. Moving. Open water. You lie in the current and let it go over you, and drink, and drink. When the rain comes back, months later, you will be able to go back up to the pond by the stream if you want to. But the river is the road now.

choices.text: The tortoise stops on the bank and looks at it first

effects.log: The tortoise looks at the river for a long time before it goes in, the way you look at something you are going to know for a very long time. The snake, for once, waits.

events.text: The people of the river have started to call you something. The ferry hands at the landing call you the Old One, though you are not old, because you sit so still under the landing. The children at the weirs call you the Two-Mouth, because of the snake. The washerwomen call you the Temple Turtle, because they have heard the story. You are one creature with three names, and none of them is yours.

choices.text: The tortoise likes the Old One

effects.log: The Old One. The tortoise turns it over and finds it fits. The snake says it makes you sound like a stone. The tortoise says yes.

choices.text: The snake likes the Two-Mouth

effects.log: The Two-Mouth. It is rude, and true, and the snake loves it. The tortoise says it makes you sound like a liar. The snake says yes.

choices.text: Neither: a name should come from inside

effects.log: Neither of you wants a name the river gave you. That is the first thing you agree about. It is not the last thing you need to.

events.text: The argument about the name goes on for a year. The tortoise wants something slow and plain, that you could carve on a stone. The snake wants something quick and clever, that you could say to a stranger and watch them work out. Every name one head offers, the other head finds the flaw in. You are getting very good at finding flaws.

choices.text: The tortoise gives way, this once

effects.log: The tortoise stops arguing. It is not agreement. The snake knows it is not, and finds no pleasure in winning, and the name it chose sits unused between you.

choices.text: The snake gives way, this once

effects.log: The snake stops arguing. It is not agreement either. The tortoise knows it, and the plain name it wanted sounds hollow, said by one head only.

choices.text: Stop looking for a name. Wait for one

effects.log: You stop. You lie under the ferry landing and let the river talk. A name will come or it will not. Even the snake can wait, if the tortoise is waiting with it.

events.text: A winter night under the ice, and the tortoise says a word half asleep, not a name, only a sound, the sound the river makes under the ferry landing. And the snake, at the same moment, says the same sound. You lie in the dark and both of you know: that is it. If you both want it. If the Knot will hold it.

choices.text: Both heads take it: one name, only yours

effects.log: You say it together, once, aloud under the ice. It is not the Old One or the Two-Mouth or the Temple Turtle. It is the first thing that has ever been only yours, and it took both of you to find it.

choices.text: Take it, and mean it

effects.log: You take it. It fits, more or less, the way a shell fits after a hard winter. Both heads use it. Both heads mean it. The river people never hear it, and never need to.

choices.text: The tortoise says: not yet, we are not ready

effects.log: The tortoise says it, and it is right, and the snake knows it is right, and hates it. The sound goes back into the river. It will come again, when the two of you are closer. Let the heads talk.

choices.text: The snake says: it is only a sound

effects.log: The snake says it is only a sound, quickly, before the tortoise can say anything else. The tortoise draws its head in. The name is gone by morning, the way a dream goes, and you are two names again.

events.text: The ice goes out all at once in the night, and the snow on the mountains comes down behind it, and the river rises brown and loud and takes everything that is not tied down: willow branches, a chicken coop, a bridge plank, you. Past the black-sand bank, past the ford, past a village, past another village, turning over and over in the dark.

choices.text: The tortoise shuts tight and lets the flood carry the shell

effects.log: Shut, tumbling, knocked against stones and roots in the brown dark. A shell is made for this. The snake, pressed flat inside the rim, is not, and says so afterwards for a week. (-8 health)

choices.text: The snake grabs a passing branch with its jaws

ok.log: The snake bites a willow branch and holds, and the branch swings into the bank, and you climb out among drowned reeds, half a day downriver and alive.

fail.log: The branch twists and nearly pulls the snake's head off. It lets go. You go on down the river, one head aching. (-12 health)

events.text: Three villages down, the flood slows into a wide brown bay, and a family is out in a little boat with a net, taking what the river brings: firewood, a pot, a drowned piglet. The net comes up with you in it. {npc}, a ferry girl of ten with a chapped face, looks at you, and at the snake, and shouts to the back of the boat: "Grandfather! It has two heads!"

choices.text: The tortoise lies quiet in the net

effects.log: The grandfather looks over the side and says a turtle in a flood is good luck, if you put it back. {npc} puts you back, with great ceremony, and says your name is Lucky. It is not. It is a start.

choices.text: The snake tangles the net so the piglet gets loose too

effects.log: The snake works the knots until half the catch goes back over the side, you and the piglet among it. The piglet, it turns out, was only nearly drowned. {npc} watches it swim to shore and laughs and laughs.

events.text: Another spring, another flood, and this time it comes over the bank of the temple pond itself, brown water through the lotus and out over the wall and down the valley, and the whole pond goes with it: turtles, carp, lotus roots, you. Down the stream, faster and faster, toward the place where the stream meets the river.

choices.text: Let it take you all the way to the river

effects.log: Down the stream and out into the big water in one long roar. When the flood drops you are in a cold side channel of the river, bruised, alone, free. The pond is up the valley still, if you ever want it. Open water. (-6 health)

choices.text: The snake catches the temple gate post as you go by

ok.log: The snake bites the gatepost and holds, and the flood goes past and down the valley without you. When it drops you are in the mud by the gate with the two pine turtles above you. The pond will fill again. You are still a pond turtle.

fail.log: The snake gets the post and loses it, and you go over the wall and down the valley anyway, and fetch up in the river bruised in both heads. Open water, whether you wanted it or not. (-10 health)

choices.text: Both heads: ride it out on a lotus root, and steer for the side channel

effects.log: The tortoise clings; the snake watches the water and says left, left, now. You come out of the flood into a quiet side channel of the river without a scratch, and look back up the valley at the place you came from, and both of you know the river is where you live now.

events.text: The bell in the pavilion above the pond is struck before dawn, and again at dusk, and the sound goes down into the water and into your shell. The snake counts the strokes: twenty-eight at dawn, it says, and thirty-three at dusk. The tortoise does not count strokes. The tortoise counts years: it has lost count somewhere after the third spring in the pond.

choices.text: The snake explains why the counts are different

effects.log: The snake has listened to the monks. Twenty-eight for the heavens, it says, thirty-three for the other heavens. The tortoise asks how many heavens there are. The snake says it depends on the time of day. It is very pleased with this.

choices.text: The tortoise feels the bell and does not count

effects.log: The sound goes into the shell and stays. The tortoise lets it. It does not need to know how many; it only needs to know that it comes, every dawn, and will come tomorrow.

events.text: A quarrel that goes on all winter. The snake says it is the seventh year in the pond, because it has counted every stroke of the bell since you came, and divided. The tortoise says it is the sixth, because it has counted winters. One of you is wrong. You are one body. It is maddening.

choices.text: The tortoise holds to its count

effects.log: Six winters. The tortoise is sure. The snake is sure too. Neither gives way, and in spring the monks paint the date on the new lantern, and neither of you can read it.

choices.text: The snake holds to its count

effects.log: The snake recounts aloud, stroke by stroke, all seven years of them. It takes a month. The tortoise falls asleep in the second year of it.

choices.text: Both heads work it out together

effects.log: The snake counted strokes from the first dawn; the tortoise counted winters from the first winter. You came to the pond in the spring. Both counts are right, measured from different ends. It is the most important thing the two of you have learned so far, and it is about a bell.

events.text: The last night of the year, and the bell is struck one hundred and eight times, slowly, one for each of the troubles that bind a living thing, the monks say, so that the new year can begin without them. The whole valley comes up the path with lanterns to listen. The snake counts. The tortoise does not. Both of you hear the last stroke at the same moment.

choices.text: The tortoise lets each stroke take something away

effects.log: One hundred and eight. The tortoise lets each one go through the shell and out the other side, and takes something with it each time: the heron, the basket, the cold. At the end the shell feels lighter than it has since the egg.

choices.text: The snake keeps every stroke, and counts what each one was

effects.log: One for the heron. One for the cold under the ice. One for every field the snake never walked. The snake does not let a single one go. It files them all, very neatly, and feels heavier, and better.

events.text: A frog on the bank of the side stream, small and green and very sure of itself, asks to ride across on your shell. Its own legs are tired, it says, and there is a heron downstream, and you look like a boat. The snake looks at it the way snakes look at frogs.

choices.text: The tortoise says yes

effects.log: The frog hops on and sits between the snake's coils as if it owned them. You swim it across, slowly, with the snake staring at it the whole way. It hops off on the far side and does not say thank you. Frogs do not.

choices.text: The snake says yes, in a friendly voice

effects.log: The frog looks at the snake, and at the snake's friendly voice, and decides it is not that tired after all. It swims. The snake is disappointed. The tortoise is a little proud of the frog.

events.text: The frog again, with a friend, and the friend's cousin. Word has gone round the side stream that the turtle with two heads carries frogs across, and today there are six of them on the bank, and the snake has not eaten since yesterday.

choices.text: Carry them all. A bridge does not choose

effects.log: Six frogs, one at a time, across and back. The snake goes hungry and silent and does not eat one. It takes all afternoon. That evening the tortoise brings the snake to the best snail bed it knows, and the snake understands it as an apology.

choices.text: Carry five

effects.log: Five frogs across. The sixth was a little slow getting off. The other five never ride your shell again, and the tortoise has a long think about what kind of bridge eats its passengers.

choices.text: Both heads: carry them all, then hunt on the far bank, where no frog asked anything

effects.log: Six frogs carried, every one. Then over on the far bank, among strangers, the snake eats well. A bridge keeps faith with the ones who ride it. The rest of the river is the rest of the river.

events.text: A summer storm, the side stream up and roaring, and on the near bank a whole bank of small creatures stranded by the water: frogs, a shrew, three beetles, a baby water rail. The far bank is dry. You are the only thing in the stream that does not mind the current.

choices.text: Be a bridge: lie in the current and let them cross on your back

effects.log: You wedge yourself between two stones in the middle of the flood with your shell just above the water, and they cross, one by one, scrabbling, over your back. It takes half the night. It is the first time you are a bridge. It is not the last. (-6 health)

choices.text: The snake ferries the little ones in its mouth, gently

effects.log: The snake carries the beetles and the shrew across one by one in its mouth, very gently, and does not eat a single thing. The tortoise has never seen it so careful. Nor has the shrew.

events.text: A winter morning, a frozen puddle at the edge of the pond, and in it, looking up at you, a turtle you do not know. The shell is darker than it was, no longer brown, nearly black, the plates edged like tiles on a roof. Round it, a black snake, thicker than a thread now, as thick as a finger. Both heads look at their reflection for a long time.

choices.text: The tortoise studies the plates of the shell

effects.log: Thirteen plates on the back, the tortoise counts, each one a little hexagon, blank and black. It does not know why it counts them. It feels as if each one is waiting for something to be written on it.

choices.text: The snake admires itself

effects.log: A finger thick, black as ink, a fine bright eye. The snake looks at itself in the ice for a very long time. The tortoise lets it. It is, honestly, a handsome snake.

choices.text: Both heads look at the one creature in the ice

effects.log: Not a tortoise with a snake on it. Not a snake with a tortoise in it. One dark creature in the ice, with two heads, looking up. You have never seen yourself whole before. Neither of you says anything. Neither of you needs to.

events.text: Pilgrims at the pond in the spring point at you, and an old man among them, a scholar by his hat, looks for a long time and says to his grandson: "Black. A black tortoise with a snake. Do you know what that is, in the old books? It is the guardian of the north." The grandson says it is a turtle in a pond. Both are right, for now.

choices.text: The tortoise remembers the words: guardian of the north

effects.log: Guardian of the north. The tortoise does not know what the north is, or what a guardian does. It keeps the words anyway, the way it keeps every word it is given. Some things you keep before you understand them.

choices.text: The snake decides the grandson is right

effects.log: A turtle in a pond. The snake prefers that. A turtle in a pond is not wanted by fortune-tellers or scholars or anyone with a brazier. It hopes very much that it stays a turtle in a pond for a long time. It will not.
